articles.title: Dinner party has guests bringing tables, dressing in white and learning location last-minute
articles.summary: Detroit's Dîner en Blanc returns with a secret outdoor dining location revealed only moments before guests in white attire arrive for the elegant picnic.
articles.body: Revelers in Detroit will gather tonight for Dîner en Blanc, an international dining phenomenon in which guests dress entirely in white and gather for an elaborate picnic at a location that remains secret until shortly before the event. Detroit’s first official Dîner en Blanc, held outside Michigan Central Station on July 26, 2025, drew close to 1,000 guests. GLP-1 BOOM COULD RESHAPE RESTAURANT BARS AS DINERS CUT BACK ON ALCOHOL The city’s inaugural event "quickly became one of the city’s most talked-about social gatherings," Michigan.org reported, with local celebrities and members of the media among those who gathered "for a night of elegance beneath the summer sky." Tickets for this year’s Detroit dinner range from $52 to $77 per person and are sold in pairs. A $52 ticket requires guests to bring their own table and chairs, while a $67 option includes a table and chairs. A $77 option includes bus transportation but requires guests to bring their own table and chairs. A $14 membership fee also applies to each ticket. Detroit is one of more than 80 cities around the world that have hosted Dîner en Blanc, with U.S. editions taking place in cities including New York, Philadelphia, Chicago, Washington, D.C., Atlanta, Miami and New Orleans. Dîner en Blanc traces its origins to Paris in 1988, when François Pasquier organized a picnic for friends after his family returned to the city following several years in Tahiti. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Our garden was too small, so we decided to host a picnic in the Bois de Boulogne," Pasquier recalled in a 2018 interview published on the official Dîner en Blanc Paris website. "To make it easier to find each other, we agreed to dress all in white." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Pasquier said the dinner proved so successful that the group repeated it the following year, and attendance eventually grew to more than 1,000 people. The 30th anniversary edition of Le Dîner en Blanc de Paris, held on the Esplanade des Invalides in June 2018, included a record-breaking 17,000 guests. Part of the tradition is holding the dinner in a public space not normally intended to accommodate such a large gathering. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "It must be carefully controlled for everyone’s safety and so that the city will allow us to hold future editions," the organization said. The destination is kept under wraps as guests make their way to designated meeting spots throughout the city. From there, volunteer table leaders guide groups to the final location, according to the event’s website. The secretiveness of the location adds "an air of mystery and excitement to this festive, community-focused picnic," according to Michigan.org. The suggested dress code is "crisp linen, dreamy lace [and] bold accessories." Gold, silver or nude accents are allowed, but partygoers are encouraged to keep their outfits "mostly en blanc," with specific instructions for "no ivory, no off-white and no beige." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Depending on their ticket package, guests traditionally arrive with folding tables and chairs, along with white tablecloths and napkins, tableware, food and a garbage bag for cleaning up afterward. On-site rentals and catered meals are also available in some cities, and guests are encouraged to be creative and "go all-out" with décor — white, of course.

articles.title: A Mexican entrepreneur began melting discarded plastic into wall and roof panels; within three years his startup had built 500 rooms and secured contracts for 300 homes
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Workers at a recycling plant in central Mexico are turning five and a half tonnes of discarded plastic bottles and old toys every day into strong buil.
articles.body: Workers at a recycling plant in central Mexico are turning five and a half tonnes of discarded plastic bottles and old toys every day into strong building materials, helping low-income families get better homes while keeping waste out of local dumps. The process, developed in 2013 by social enterprise EcoDom in Puebla state, turns melted plastic waste into strong wall and roofing panels. Within three years of starting operations, the company had built 500 rooms for municipal housing programmes and won public contracts to construct 300 complete homes across nearby towns. A report by media organisation Unreasonable Group explains how founder Carlos Daniel González created the company to tackle two problems at the same time: pollution and a serious shortage of affordable housing. González grew up in Puebla, where government figures and regional data cited by Unreasonable Group show that 64 per cent of people live in poverty. He saw the effects of unmanaged waste around him from an early age. “As a kid, I remember seeing all of the plastic and the contamination it caused, for us and for the animals,” said González. “I've always cared about the environment, so I decided I had to create and lead a solution.”Turning waste into building panelsMexico is the world’s 12th-largest consumer of plastic and produces more than five million tonnes of plastic waste each year. The World Bank estimates that 11.5 million Mexicans live in extreme poverty on $1.25 or less a day, leaving many people without safe and basic housing. “I live in a place with a lot of poverty and problems of marginalization,” said González. “Some people live in truly deplorable conditions, places you can't even call houses. My vision is very clear. I have the conviction to help the most people I can have a dignified life by getting rid of extreme poverty, cleaning up my country at the same time.” To make the building panels, workers collect different types of used plastic and sort them to remove materials that could release toxic fumes when heated. A machine then cuts the selected plastic into small, even pieces before workers place them in industrial ovens heated to 350 degrees Celsius. After 30 minutes in the oven, the melted plastic is moved into a hydraulic press. The machine compresses the material and turns it into solid panels measuring about 2.4 metres long, 1.2 metres wide and 2.5 centimetres thick. The Puebla factory produces 120 panels a day, recycling tonnes of waste that would otherwise likely end up in landfills. A complete 40-square-metre home needs 80 panels and includes two bedrooms, a bathroom, a living area and a kitchen. “It only takes seven days to build a house that uses two tons of plastic,” said González. He also pointed to the strength and other benefits of the finished material, saying: “[A house] keeps you warm, the costs are low, it's great for the environment, and it will last 100 years without falling apart. These are just some of our value propositions.”Affordable homes through local governmentsEcoDom does not work only as a private construction company. It supplies building panels directly to local governments and non-governmental organisations involved in subsidised social housing programmes. Prices recorded by Unreasonable Group show that roof panels cost 600 Mexican pesos ($33), exterior wall panels cost 650 pesos ($36), and interior panels cost 500 pesos ($28). Through government housing programmes, eligible low-income families pay about 5,000 pesos ($280) for a finished two-room home. The first major municipal project began in Huauchinango, Puebla, where the local government hired EcoDom to provide panels for 500 room extensions. Each extension covered about 135 square feet. After that project, officials in Chiconcuautla hired the company to build 150 separate homes measuring 460 square feet each. A second agreement of the same size was later signed with authorities in Pahuatlán for another 150 homes. The company’s work has also created a new supply chain that is changing how informal waste collectors earn money in the region.Better pay for informal waste collectorsInformal waste collectors in Mexico have traditionally received very little money from commercial recycling companies. Some earn as little as 1.5 pesos, or six cents, for every kilogram of plastic they collect. To maintain a reliable supply of plastic for its factory, EcoDom created buying agreements that pay local collectors much more. By offering better prices per kilogram, the company has nearly doubled the earnings of some independent waste collectors in the region. The system also helps provide the factory with its daily supply of five and a half tonnes of plastic, keeping the material out of landfills and waterways. According to information cited by Unreasonable Group, less than five per cent of plastic made worldwide is recovered or kept out of landfills. Between 10 million and 20 million tonnes of plastic enter the oceans each year, with some types of synthetic material taking up to 1,000 years to break down.Taking the model beyond PueblaAfter setting up its operations in Puebla, González said he wants to increase factory production, secure larger national contracts and eventually bring the building model to other countries facing similar housing shortages. “This has the potential to grow exponentially,” said González. “The problem of trash is huge in my country. In the whole world, there's a ton of trash. In the next year, I want to grow the company ten-fold. First, we will concentrate in Mexico, but in 3-5 years, we want to go to other countries. There is poverty everywhere. The world is a house for everyone, and it's worth it to fight for expanding this business. I will dedicate the rest of my life to this.” The company’s production records and agreements with local governments show how low-cost recycling technology, combined with public housing support, can turn waste into useful and long-lasting homes for communities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2019, man began carving a two-storey family home into a China mountain; after 7 years battling water leaks, fault lines and humidity, he finally makes it livable
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A man in Sichuan, China, has spent seven years transforming a raw sandstone cliff into a two-storey home for his family, using his experience in coal .
articles.body: A man in Sichuan, China, has spent seven years transforming a raw sandstone cliff into a two-storey home for his family, using his experience in coal mining and construction to carve rooms, stairs and furniture directly into the mountain. The extraordinary project survived water leaks, heavy storms, structural challenges and a two-year hiatus that allowed nature to reclaim parts of the property.According to Quantum Makers, the project began in 2019, when the man, identified in the video as Hu Ge or Mr. Hu, decided to build a family home unlike a conventional brick-and-mortar house. Instead of constructing on the mountain, he chose to carve directly into it.His plan was ambitious: create a ground-floor bedroom and living space for himself and his wife, then excavate a second level for his two children and connect both floors with an internal staircase.With years of experience in coal mining and construction, he understood how rock could behave under pressure. But working inside a mountain still presented risks, with thousands of tonnes of sandstone above him and hidden cracks potentially threatening the entire structure.He left a giant rock pillar to support the ceilingThe excavation began on the lower level, where he used drilling equipment to remove sections of sandstone. Rather than clearing the entire space immediately, he left a massive central pillar in place to support the ceiling.He then shaped the surrounding ceiling into an arch so the weight could be transferred towards the side walls. Once the structure was stable, he removed the pillar.Even the discarded rock found another purpose. Some of the cylindrical pieces produced during drilling were saved for later use, while part of the large supporting pillar was turned into a garden table.Water became one of his biggest challengesRain proved to be one of the most serious threats to the mountain home. While excavating the bedroom, he noticed a draft coming through the rock, indicating the presence of cracks.He created a drainage trench to direct water towards the entrance and sealed the cracks with cement. But heavy storms later exposed the weakness of the system.Water began pouring through the mountain, overwhelming the drainage system and forcing him to reinforce the area with additional cement and expanding foam. He also left ventilation openings because completely sealing the rock could trap humidity inside.The experience became an early warning of the challenges he would face maintaining a home carved into the humid Sichuan landscape.He brought electricity and spring water into the mountainMaking the cave livable required more than carving rooms. He personally dragged electrical cable through the forest to bring power to the remote property.For water, he found a natural spring roughly a mile away and developed a system to pump the water to a storage tank near the house. Pipes were laid through the forest, including along a significant elevation drop.The system eventually supplied the home with running water for the bathroom and other facilities.When water pressure later proved too weak for the shower, he moved the storage system higher into the forest, allowing gravity to increase the pressure.He carved a kitchen, terrace and staircase into the mountainAs the lower floor took shape, he began creating an outdoor kitchen directly from the rock. The roof of the kitchen also served as a terrace, providing a platform from which he could work on the second floor.He used trees removed from the site as structural supports for the porch and drilled sockets directly into the rock to secure horizontal beams.The kitchen itself featured separate combustion areas for cooking and boiling water, while a natural crack in the rock was adapted into a chimney.He also carved an external staircase from the sandstone and installed a railing to make the area safer for his children.The most difficult task was connecting the two floorsAfter more than two years of excavation, the project reached one of its biggest engineering challenges: creating the internal staircase.He initially carved part of the staircase from the lower floor but eventually decided to excavate the upper section first and connect the two sections from opposite directions.The task required precise measurements because even a small error could prevent the two sections from meeting.After years of work, his calculations proved successful. The staircase connected the two floors, turning the separate excavated spaces into a single two-storey home.A hidden fault line threatened the projectThe second floor brought another major surprise when excavation revealed a large natural fissure running behind sections of the walls.He worried that the crack could be connected to the water problems on the lower floor and potentially allow water into the house or compromise the structure.To understand the fissure, he conducted a smoke test by burning wood inside it. The smoke escaped through an existing outlet, suggesting there were no obvious dangerous fractures extending through the structure.However, the test left the studio covered in soot and forced him to restore the room.Rather than continue excavating into the unstable area, he changed his plans and stopped expanding that section.He even made furniture from the mountain itselfThe unusual home was designed to minimise the need to bring heavy furniture into the remote location. On the upper level, he carved a workspace directly into the sandstone.A central section became a desk, while carefully positioned openings provided ventilation and natural light.He also incorporated drainage into the design, drilling passages at a slight downward angle so rainwater could escape.Throughout the project, he repeatedly reused materials rather than discarding them, turning leftover rock into garden structures and using salvaged materials wherever possible.After seven years, nature nearly swallowed his workJust as the mountain home was approaching completion, an unexpected personal matter forced him to leave the project for almost two years.When he eventually returned, he found the property dramatically changed.Sichuan's humidity had taken its toll. Mold had spread, a wooden bed had rotted and vegetation had begun covering the exterior. Roots and vines had grown across the rock facade, making it difficult to distinguish the house from the surrounding mountain.Instead of abandoning the project, he treated the damage as a test of the home's durability and began rebuilding and upgrading the property.He replaced the waste system and restored the kitchenOne of his first tasks after returning was replacing the deteriorated bathroom waste system with a proper septic tank designed to accommodate his family of four.He repaired the stairs and began restoring the outdoor kitchen, which had also been heavily overtaken by nature.The chimney was raised to around 13 feet after earlier testing revealed smoke leaks and sparks near the bamboo forest. A cover was added to prevent rain from entering.He then restored the kitchen's water supply, installed a shut-off valve and made the area more practical for everyday use.The mountain home is now livableAfter years of drilling, excavation and rebuilding, the home now has many of the essentials of a conventional house, including electricity, running water, bathroom facilities, a kitchen, heating, Wi-Fi and sleeping areas.He replaced the damaged wooden bed with an iron one better suited to the humid environment and installed a steel stove to help keep the interior warm and dry.Solar-powered lights were also installed around the courtyard and pathways, while a small pool was created for his children.The upper floor, meanwhile, remains a work in progress as he continues excavating and expanding the space intended for his children.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: FBI lowers hiring bar: Getting services from prostitutes, stealing from employer, bestiality not automatic deal-breakers
articles.summary: US News: The FBI used to reject anyone if they admitted that they had hired sex workers in the past, stolen from an employer, or engaged in acts of bestiality..
articles.body: The FBI used to reject anyone if they admitted that they had hired sex workers in the past, stolen from an employer, or engaged in acts of bestiality. But now, these factors are not immediate deal-breakers, CBS reported. The FBI is willing to give candidates a pass on prostitution, as long as they have not hired sex workers three or more times. And the hiring of the sex workers must not have taken place within the last 10 years, the report said.This leeway has been allowed because a person may have hired a sex worker in a location where prostitution is legal. But a person who was in a position of "trust" who solicited sex would still be automatically disqualified from FBI employment. Examples of positions of trust are those who work in the fields of public safety, education, health, social work, finance or law. Being a member of the military was not among the listed categories, and it was not clear if they would be treated as such.Stole from employer? It's fine if it's more than three years agoUnder the new eligibility rules, a person who stole from an employer is not automatically disqualified as long as the incident occurred more than three years ago.The new standards also specifically address applicants who have engaged in past acts of bestiality or animal cruelty – saying they may still be considered for the bureau as long as the incidents took place before the age of 18.In a statement, an FBI spokesperson denied that the bureau is allowing people who have a history of criminal sexual acts to work there, and said the FBI "has and always will maintain some of the highest suitability standards for its applicants and employees in the US government.""Over the years, the FBI has had a number of applicants who suffered sexual abuse in their past, causing polygraph questions about prostitution, bestiality, or other similar issues to affect their polygraph through zero fault of their own," the spokesperson said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: A vessel with five people on board is "in distress" in the English Channel, the coastguard says.
articles.body:
A vessel with five people on board is "in distress" in the English Channel, the coastguard has said.

A search and rescue helicopter and boats have been launched to try to help the vessel south west of Eddystone Lighthouse off Plymouth, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency said.

It said it was alerted just after 18:00 BST and a coastguard rescue helicopter and a fixed wing aircraft have been sent, together with RNLI lifeboats from Falmouth and Plymouth.

No further details are currently available about the vessel or the nature of the emergency.

articles.title: Taylor Swift donates $50,000 to mom left with collapsed lung, ruptured organs after saving teens from highway crash
articles.summary: Taylor Swift has donated $50,000 to help a Rhode Island mother who was left seriously injured in car accident last month, NBC News has confirmed.
articles.body: Taylor Swift has donated $50,000 to help a Rhode Island mother who was left seriously injured in car accident last month, NBC News has confirmed. Ashley Taunton, a married mother of three, was driving on I-95 in Hopkinton during a torrential rainstorm on July 18 when she saw a car in front of her hydroplane off the road. She pulled over and ran to help the teenagers inside the crashed vehicle, her husband, Joe Taunton, told NBC affiliate WJAR of Providence. As she was helping them, another vehicle hydroplaned and barreled toward them, he said. “In a split-second act of pure bravery, Ashley pushed the other person out of harm’s way, taking the brunt of the impact herself,” according to an online fundraiser to support her medical bills. Joe Taunton said his wife suffered a severe leg injury and extensive internal injuries, including damage to her small and large intestines, liver lacerations and a ruptured diaphragm that caused one of her lungs to collapse. She has undergone at least three surgeries, he said. Ashley Taunton has documented her recovery on social media, sharing photos from her hospital bed while in an induced coma, with a nasogastric tube for a small bowel obstruction, staples on her stomach, and — more recently — back home in a leg brace. On Friday, she posted on Instagram about Swift’s donation, writing: “This is absolutely mind-blowing and so very humbling.” “@taylorswift you are a beautiful soul I wish I could hug you IRL. Maybe the next time your in Westerly 😘 I live 20 minutes away 🫶 Thank you Jesus for so many amazing humans. This is unbelievable and I am overwhelmed with gratitude. To God be the glory!” she wrote.

articles.title: 4 at hydel unit among 108 Indians rescued; toll 682
articles.summary: South Asia News: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): Death toll from the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster rose to 675 in Nepal on Saturday evening, with 2,426 people still .
articles.body: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): Death toll from the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster rose to 675 in Nepal on Saturday evening, with 2,426 people still missing as rescuers continued searching mud-filled valleys, riverbanks and hydropower tunnels three days after the catastrophic flood. National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said 2,498 people had been rescued, 219 were injured and more than 18,700 personnel deployed for search and rescue.Across the border in Tibet, Chinese authorities reported seven deaths and 554 people missing at Gyirong port as of early Saturday, taking the confirmed toll on the two sides to at least 682.Indian authorities revised down the number of Indian nationals unaccounted for in Nepal to 287 on Saturday evening from 320 a day earlier as more people were traced. Ministry of external affairs (MEA) said another 128 of Indian origin who held other nationalities remained uncontactable. No confirmed figure for Indian deaths has been announced by MEA.The ministry said 88 Indian nationals had been rescued, including four workers brought out from a hydropower project in Rasuwa on Saturday. They are expected to reach Kathmandu soon.With India having sent relief in three military transport aircraft, Nepal finance minister Swarnim Wagle said, “PM Modi and MEA have been very positive about expressing their solidarity and pledging any amount of support that Nepal needs... They’ve also been concerned about Indian pilgrims who have been stranded, their rescue is also a priority for us.”India also working to bring back citizens stranded on Chinese sideA specialised Indian reconnaissance team surveyed flood-hit tunnels at Chilime and Langtang with Nepal army before a larger tunnel-rescue team and equipment were sent in.Nepalese tourism authorities maintained a separate and broader rescue database. Nepal tourism board said 261 foreign nationals and tourists had been rescued by 6pm Saturday, including 167 Indians and 40 Chinese, while 320 foreign nationals remained “out of communication”. The difference between Indian and Nepalese figures reflected separate lists being maintained by tourism, diplomatic and rescue agencies as names continued to be reconciled.India was also working to bring back nationals stranded on the Chinese side of the border. MEA said 120 Indians crossed from Tibet into Nepal Saturday. A day earlier, India had said around 400 Indians, many of them Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrims, had been located on the Chinese side and were safe.The scale of those still unaccounted for in Nepal remained dominated by people trapped at hydropower projects and along the flood corridor. NDRRMA’s missing list included 933 workers from hydropower projects as well as foreign tourists, security personnel and employees of customs and immigration offices. Searches continued inside and around several tunnels where workers were believed trapped.Rescue operations were repeatedly complicated by unstable slopes and concern over barrier lakes formed after the glacier collapse. By Saturday, Chinese hydrological teams said one major debris-dammed lake had largely begun draining naturally, reducing the immediate threat of a catastrophic breach, though authorities continued monitoring unstable debris and surrounding slopes for fresh landslides or mudslides.In Gyirong, Chinese authorities said 554 people remained missing after the glacier-triggered mudslide devastated the border port. China had evacuated 555 tourists and moved 499 villagers and construction workers to safer locations, while professional rescue teams continued searches in mud that was more than 1.5m deep in parts of the core disaster zone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
